angle: I was a BDR with 5 tools and a spreadsheet. Prioritizing my accounts took 10 hours a month
post_first_line: Neema Zarrabian lost 10 hours monthly prioritizing accounts.
linkedin_post:
Neema Zarrabian lost 10 hours monthly prioritizing accounts.

The workflow behind those hours is worth a closer look.

Six years ago, Neema Zarrabian was a BDR working with an intent tool, a sequencing tool, a data tool, Sales Navigator, and a spreadsheet. Every single day meant combing through all of them.

The first 2 hours of the day went to finding data and writing emails. The last 2 hours went to setting up the call list for the next day.

Then came reprioritizing. Looking through new accounts and ranking them took 10 hours every month.

None of it was strategy. It was manual stitching between tools that never talked to each other.

That's the problem we think about at Unify. Reps shouldn't spend their best hours moving data between tabs.

What's the most manual part of your day?

takeaways: Running five tools plus a spreadsheet creates daily manual work that hides in plain sight.
Prep tasks like finding data and building call lists can take up 4 hours a day.
Account prioritization done by hand adds up to 10 hours every month.
lesson.exercise: Track one week of your workday in 30-minute blocks. Label each block as selling or tool-juggling, then pick the biggest tool-juggling block to simplify first.

angle: It took 6-8 discovery calls to learn my target account was unintentionally breaking the law
post_first_line: Six to eight discovery calls. That's what it took.
linkedin_post:
Six to eight discovery calls. That's what it took.

Neema Zarrabian had one account on the list that was impossible to stop thinking about.

Five years ago, Neema Zarrabian lived in the Boston area and wanted to break into a large school district. The goal was to understand why they would need Unify's product.

The answer didn't show up online. It surfaced through discovery, over 6 to 8 calls, when the district's chief of human resources shared a problem tied to teacher-to-student ratios.

The account had a compliance issue it hadn't intended to create.

Neema Zarrabian's takeaway: research with Unify Chats could probably have surfaced news about it much faster. But the real insight came from a conversation with the right person.

When you have 30 enterprise accounts to break into in a quarter, or a named account list with one account you're set on, the pattern holds. Research gets you in the door. The buyer tells you what's actually going on.

What's the best thing a buyer ever told you on a call?

lesson.title: Discovery Finds What Research Can't
takeaways: Some of the most valuable account insights never appear online and only come from conversations with the right person.
Research can speed up how you find signals and news, but discovery calls uncover the context behind them.
Persistence on a named account pays off when you keep asking questions until the real problem surfaces.
lesson.exercise: Pick one named account you haven't cracked. List three questions you'd ask a senior stakeholder in a discovery call that no online research could answer, then book one call to ask them.

angle: Outbound has two broken paths: 50 browser tabs or tens of hours building one workflow
linkedin_post:
50 browser tabs open at once.
That's what outbound looks like for most reps.

Outbound usually splits into two paths, and both are broken.

Path one: AEs and SDRs working out of Salesforce reports and LinkedIn Sales Nav, with a Chrome extension to pull contact info. The workflow is extremely manual. You sift through each data point one by one, bouncing across tabs.

Path two: GTM engineers building very complicated workflows in a tool like Unify or Clay. You have to connect every data point and decide what happens in every column.

One side drowns in manual work. The other side takes on a heavy build before anything ships.

Neither path gets reps to the right account quickly.

Which path does your team live on today?

Slide 8: Which path is your team stuck on?

lesson.title: The two broken paths of outbound
takeaways: Reps working from Salesforce reports, Sales Nav, and Chrome extensions end up with an extremely manual workflow and around 50 tabs open.
GTM engineers building in tools like Unify or Clay have to decide what happens with every data point and every column.
Both paths cost time: one in daily manual effort, the other in upfront workflow building.
lesson.exercise: Map your outbound process this week. Count the tools and tabs a rep touches per account, and list the data points a workflow would need a decision for. See which path you're really on.

angle: Five minutes before a call: how an AE preps with recent news and growth signals instead of org-charting on LinkedIn
post_first_line: $300 million ARR. Series D. One prompt.
linkedin_post:
$300 million ARR. Series D. One prompt.

Neema Zarrabian shared how an AE preps in the five minutes before a call without opening LinkedIn.

The scenario: a call with Vanta is about to start. There's no time to org chart the company, map out verticals, find the CRO or VP of sales, or count BDRs.

Instead, the ask is simple: find all the recent news that's relevant, so the call starts with a point of view on where we can help.

The results in that example:

Vanta is already launching identity trust platforms, which aligns with how our business thinks about the space.

They just announced a Series D and crossed $300 million ARR. That signals growth, and more investment in growth.

Every data point comes with the exact timestamp. You can query for the exact sources and read the article if you want to.

It also helps answer a key question: are they prioritizing enterprise or SMB?

The shift: prep stops being a research project and becomes a point of view you walk in with.

What do you check first before a call?
carousel: Slide 1: Five minutes before a call. No time for LinkedIn.
Slide 2: Skip the org chart, the verticals, and the BDR headcount.
Slide 3: Ask for recent news that's relevant to the call.
Slide 4: Walk in with a point of view on where you can help.
Slide 5: Series D and $300 million ARR signal growth investment.
Slide 6: Every data point comes with a timestamp and a source.
Slide 7: Read the article if you want the full context.
Slide 8: Know if they're prioritizing enterprise or SMB.

lesson.title: Five-minute call prep with news and growth signals
takeaways: Org-charting on LinkedIn is slow; recent news gives you a point of view faster.
Funding and ARR milestones signal that a company is investing in growth.
Timestamps and sources let you verify any claim before you use it on a call.
lesson.exercise: Before your next call, spend five minutes finding recent news on the account. Write one sentence on where you can help, and note whether they're prioritizing enterprise or SMB.

angle: Which AI tool I use for CRM reporting and which for call analysis, and why I split them
post_first_line: Neema Zarrabian split AI work into two tools.
linkedin_post:
Neema Zarrabian split AI work into two tools.

One handles CRM reporting. The other handles call analysis. The reason for the split is simple.

Neema Zarrabian moved all Salesforce reporting into Unify: win rates, conversion rates, and metrics on the BDR team. Claude used to handle that.

Claude now does the bulk querying of the call recorder, pulling what was said on each call.

The pipeline work lives in Unify too. Slicing the TAM in different ways. Looking at the accounts the team isn't reaching out to. Queuing up good accounts for BDRs. Reviewing AE deals.

The pattern: match the tool to where the data lives. Reporting and account selection sit next to the CRM and TAM. Call questions sit next to the transcripts.

One tool for everything sounds tidy. Two tools for two jobs works better.

lesson.title: Split AI tools by job, not by hype
takeaways: Reporting and account selection belong near your CRM and TAM data.
Call analysis belongs in a tool that can query many transcripts in bulk.
Reviewing which tool you default to can show where a split would help.

angle: 60-70% open rates, one meeting: why open rate is the wrong number to watch
linkedin_post:
60-70% open rates. One meeting.

That gap tells you which number actually matters.

A question came in recently: about 250 companies, one to three touches so far, open rates around sixty to seventy percent, and only one reply that turned into a meeting. When do you change the messaging? Do you wait for 7+ touches?

Internally, we focus a lot less on open rates as a performance metric. We focus on reply rates.

So the intuition behind the question was right. Don't celebrate the opens. Work on bringing the reply rate up.

Here's what we're doing about it: we're working a lot on the copywriting skills the agent has access to, so the copy keeps getting better.

But the usual move is simpler. Make the message as specific as possible.

An open just means someone saw your subject line. A reply means the message gave them a reason to answer.

What metric are you watching that isn't moving revenue?

Slide 2: Opens tell you the subject line worked.
Slide 3: Replies tell you the message worked.
Slide 4: We focus a lot less on open rates internally.
Slide 5: Reply rate is the number to bring up.
Slide 6: We keep improving the copywriting skills our agent uses.
Slide 7: The usual fix: make the message as specific as possible.
Slide 8: Stop celebrating opens. Start earning replies.

lesson.title: Open rate is not the metric to optimize
takeaways: High open rates with almost no replies means the subject line works but the message doesn't.
Focus on reply rate as the performance metric, not open rate.
Make your copy as specific as possible to lift replies.
lesson.exercise: Pull your last campaign and compare open rate to reply rate. Rewrite the first two lines of your email to be more specific to the recipient, then test it against the original.
